name: In the right-hand part
why: At every step, at least one half of the window is sorted. Compare a[lo] with a[mid] to find out which half. Then check whether the target is inside that sorted half.

name: In the left-hand part
why: 18 is in the left part of the list. If your search went right, the check for 'the target is inside the sorted half' is probably missing one of its two comparisons: a[lo] <= target < a[mid].

name: Not in the list
why: 13 is in the gap between the two sorted parts. The window must still become empty, so every branch must make it smaller.

name: Not rotated at all
why: A list that is not rotated is still allowed. Code that first looks for the drop in values, and assumes there is one, fails here.

name: Rotated by one, target first
why: The left part is a single value. When lo == mid, the left half a[lo..mid] has one value, so it counts as sorted. Use a[lo] <= a[mid], with <=, not <.

name: Rotated so the smallest is last
why: The right part is a single value at the very end. Check that the branch for the right half can reach hi itself.

name: One value
why: With one value, lo, mid and hi are all the same. The loop must still run once, so use lo <= hi.

name: Empty list
why: There is nothing to search. Do not read a[0] or a[-1] before checking that the list has values.

name: Two values
why: mid rounds down to index 0, so the left half is just [9]. The target is not in it, so the search must move right with lo = mid + 1.

name: A million values, at most 80 reads
why: This list counts reads. If you find the rotation point by going through the list, or search with `in` or `.index()`, you read hundreds of thousands of values. Each pass of a binary search reads at most three: a[lo], a[mid] and a[hi].

name: A million values, target not in the list
why: The target is not in the list, and it is bigger than every value. Going through the list one by one reads all million values before it gives up.
